approachQuestion.prompt:
A device accepts every unsigned integer code in the inclusive interval [L,R]. Return the bitwise AND of all accepted codes.

Constraints: 0 <= L <= R < 2^W; 1 <= W <= 64. The interval is given by its endpoints, not as an array.
Example: W=8, L=26, R=30 -> 24. Edge case: W=8, L=7, R=7 -> 7.

Choose the best approach under these constraints.
constraints: Analyze W as a width parameter in a word-RAM model: a W-bit logical shift, comparison or bitwise operation costs constant time. Shifting a word by W is defined as zero.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

options.text: Copy L and R into two scalars. Logically shift both right until equal, counting shifts; shift the common value back left by that count.
options.feedback: Every bit below the first differing position takes a zero somewhere in the interval. Only the common leading prefix survives.

options.text: Visit every integer in the interval and accumulate their AND, using a nonwrapping loop counter.
options.feedback: This is correct on the entire domain, including R at the maximum word, but work can grow with the number of codes rather than their width.
For L=5, R=7, endpoints give 5, but the included value 6 clears bit zero, so the correct result is 4.
For L=R=7, this returns zero although the interval AND is 7.

feedback.reason: Any bit below the shared endpoint prefix changes somewhere inside the inclusive range and therefore cannot remain in the AND.
details: Compare shifted copies of the endpoints until they share the same remaining prefix. Record the number of removed low bits and restore those positions as zeros. A zero common prefix yields zero even when all W bits were removed.

Any bit below the shared endpoint prefix changes somewhere inside the inclusive range and therefore cannot remain in the AND. Shift until endpoints agree and restore removed positions as zero. Equal endpoints need no shifts.

“Copy L and R into two scalars. Logically shift both right until equal, counting shifts; shift the common value back left by that count.”: Every bit below the first differing position takes a zero somewhere in the interval. Only the common leading prefix survives.

“Visit every integer in the interval and accumulate their AND, using a nonwrapping loop counter.”: This is correct on the entire domain, including R at the maximum word, but work can grow with the number of codes rather than their width.
“Return L AND R.”: For L=5, R=7, endpoints give 5, but the included value 6 clears bit zero, so the correct result is 4.
“Return L XOR R.”: For L=R=7, this returns zero although the interval AND is 7.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For align-common-prefix, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Analyze the worst case as a function of W.
constraints: Analyze W as a width parameter in a word-RAM model: a W-bit logical shift, comparison or bitwise operation costs constant time. Shifting a word by W is defined as zero.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

feedback.reason: At most W endpoint shifts retain only copied words and a counter.
details: The two endpoints may require W logical shifts before becoming equal. The loop has only two copied words, a shift counter and the result.
Analyze W as a width parameter in a word-RAM model: a W-bit logical shift, comparison or bitwise operation costs constant time. Shifting a word by W is defined as zero.
“O(R-L+1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: That describes enumerating the interval, not the fixed endpoint method.
“O(W) time, O(W) auxiliary space”: The method retains a few word scalars, not one entry per bit.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The specified loop may remove all W positions.
